title: Byte-Swap a Register (Endianness)
statement:
Multi-byte registers do not all agree on which byte comes first. A sensor
read out over I2C or SPI often hands you its bytes **most-significant
first**, while the CPU you are running on very likely stores a 32-bit value
**least-significant byte first** in memory. Assemble the bytes the naive way
and the value is right only by accident; the fix is to reverse the byte
order explicitly, once, at the boundary.

## Your function

```
unsigned int swap_endian32(unsigned int value);
```

Return `value` with its four bytes in reverse order: byte 0 and byte 3 swap
places, and so do bytes 1 and 2. Bit order *within* each byte does not
change -- this moves bytes around, not bits.

`swap_endian32(0x12345678)` is `0x78563412`.

## Watch out

- Do this one byte at a time. Isolate a byte with a mask, shift it to where
  it belongs, and combine the four results with `|`. Trying to do it as one
  clever expression tends to produce something that works on the first test
  case and silently drops bits on the second.
- The function is its own inverse: swapping an already-swapped value gets
  you back where you started. That is a good way to check your own work by
  hand before you run the tests -- `swap_endian32(swap_endian32(x))` should
  always be `x`.
- This is exactly what `htonl`/`ntohl` (POSIX) or `_byteswap_ulong` (MSVC) /
  `__builtin_bswap32` (GCC, Clang) do in one call. Write it by hand here;
  reach for the intrinsic at work, where the compiler will turn it into a
  single `bswap` instruction and there is nothing to get wrong.

tests.name: a value that swaps to itself
tests.description: Every byte equals its mirrored partner, so this passes even with the byte pairs swapped backwards -- it will not catch that mistake on its own.
